name: Rastafari
line: Live naturally, speak with care and keep your eyes on Zion.

quote.text: We are going to emancipate ourselves from mental slavery because whilst others might free the body, none but ourselves can free the mind.
quote.source: Speech at Sydney, Nova Scotia, October 1937, printed in his magazine Black Man

quotes.text: Princes shall come out of Egypt; Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands unto God.
quotes.source: King James Version. The verse most often cited by early Ethiopianists and Rastafari

quotes.text: Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!
quotes.source: King James Version. Recited at Rastafari gatherings

quotes.text: God and history will remember your judgment.
quotes.source: Appeal to the League of Nations, Geneva, 30 June 1936

quotes.text: Up, you mighty race, you can accomplish what you will.
quotes.source: A rallying call of the Universal Negro Improvement Association in the 1920s, recorded in Philosophy and Opinions of Marcus Garvey

quotes.text: Look to Africa, when a black king shall be crowned, for the day of deliverance is at hand.
quotes.source: Widely repeated in the movement. No text by Garvey with these words has been found

words.usage: A short form of the Hebrew name of God, found in Psalm 68:4 of the King James Bible.

words.meaning: The movement, and the divine name
words.usage: From Ras Tafari, the title and name of Haile Selassie before he was crowned. The ending is said as the word I.
An Ethiopian noble title. Many Rastafari take it before their own name.
Used in place of me and often of we. It says that Jah is within each person and that speaker and hearer are joined.
The whole natural, upright way of living: food, speech, work, worship and the life force within them.
Food and living kept close to the earth. Usually no meat, no salt, nothing processed, and often no alcohol.
The powers that enslaved and still exploit: colonial states, police, greed and the mindset that serves them.
Africa, and Ethiopia above all. Also a state of freedom and rightness to be lived now.
The land of Zion, renamed with the sacred sound I.

words.meaning: A gathering with drums and chant; the oldest order
words.usage: The name comes from an anti-colonial movement in Uganda and Rwanda. It now names both the drumming rite and the Nyabinghi Order.
Also spelled Grounation. A meeting for drumming, chanting and reasoning, and the name of the day in April 1966 when the Emperor landed in Jamaica.
Sitting in a circle to talk through scripture, history and daily life. Everyone may speak and no one presides.
Thanks and praise to Jah, given aloud. Morning Ises begin the day.
A greeting and a state of being: things are in harmony.
Knowledge should lift a person up. No one should stand under it.
What presses a people down should not sound like up.
The word dedicate sounds like dead. A work is offered to life instead.
The sound of hate is taken out of the word and love is put in.
One of many words rebuilt around I.
Children of one Father. Used for men and for the community at large.
Rastafari women. A respected elder woman is an Empress.
First the fear the locksman stirred in respectable Jamaica, then a name worn with pride.
Kept under the Nazirite vow of Numbers 6 and likened to the mane of the Lion of Judah.
Short for Nyabinghi. A binghi can last for several days and nights.
Bass, funde and repeater. The funde keeps the steady heartbeat, the bass strikes under it and the repeater speaks over the top.

words.meaning: To sing sacred words to the drums
words.usage: Chants come from psalms, old hymns and the movement’s own verses. To chant down Babylon is to oppose it with word and sound.
The belief that spoken words shape the world, so they must be chosen carefully.
The word that closes many psalms. Used to seal a prayer or a statement.
Negusa Nagast, King of Kings, was the Ethiopian imperial title.
The first demand of the movement: that the descendants of the enslaved be brought home.

practices.name: Morning Ises
practices.instructions: Go outside or stand at an open window soon after waking. Before you look at a screen, give thanks aloud for life and for the day. Read one psalm slowly in a full voice: Psalm 1, 121 or 133 are often used. Then name three things you are grateful for. Ises means praise. The rule of this Onda is to give thanks first.
practices.why: Rastafari life begins with thanks and praise, and with the Psalms, which are read aloud with feeling. Starting the day outdoors gives it room.
variations: Read the psalm to someone in the house.
Sing it to a simple tune.
Thank the sun by name.

practices.name: Word, sound and power
practices.instructions: Choose one habit of speech to change for the day. Catch every phrase in which you make yourself small or passive, such as I have to, I am only, they made me, and say it again as a free person would. Replace one worn word with a livelier one. Rastafari treats language as power: words make a person.
practices.why: Rastafari reshaped English by changing words to carry their meaning: I and I, overstand, livity. The idea that words shape reality is a good one to try.
variations: Say I choose to instead of I have to.
Drop a negative word for a day.
Invent a better word for something.

practices.name: A cup of bush tea
practices.instructions: Make a cup of bush tea from fresh herbs: mint, lemongrass, fever grass or ginger with a little honey. Pick or buy the leaves, crush them, pour hot water and steep. Drink it outside if you can. In Jamaica bush teas are the folk remedy and the morning drink. Sip slowly, and thank the plant.
practices.why: Bush tea is a basic part of ital living, made from plants growing around the yard. It connects the morning to the earth.
variations: Grow your own mint in a pot.
Share a pot with a neighbour.
Try a new herb each week.

practices.name: Greet with blessing
practices.instructions: Greet three people today with a blessing in place of the usual hello. Say blessed love, or give thanks, or respect. Look them in the eye and mean it. In Rastafari speech a greeting is a gift, and the pronoun I and I treats the other as the same as yourself. Notice how people react.
practices.why: Greeting with a blessing treats every person as part of one family. The rule of this Onda is to meet every person as I and I.
variations: Greet a stranger with blessed love.
Answer your phone with a blessing.
End a message with one love.

practices.name: Feet on the earth
practices.instructions: Take off your shoes and stand on the ground for ten minutes: grass, soil, sand or a stone step. Wiggle your toes and breathe. Feel the temperature and the texture. Stay close to the earth is a rule of this Onda. If it is too cold, stand on a warm floor by a window and imagine the ground beneath.
practices.why: Rastafari livity centres on closeness to the natural world. Walking barefoot on the earth is a gentle way to feel it.
variations: Walk barefoot on grass.
Stand in the rain for a minute.
Plant a seed with bare hands.

practices.name: Fresh fruit and juice
practices.instructions: Start with fruit: cut up whatever is in season, mango, pineapple, papaya, banana, orange, and squeeze a glass of juice. Eat slowly and give thanks. Ital eating favours fresh, whole, natural food straight from the earth. Share the fruit with someone if you can, and leave nothing wasted.
practices.why: Ital food is fresh and whole, with plenty of fruit. A fruit breakfast is a simple, happy way to practise it.
variations: Add a spoon of coconut.
Try a fruit you have not eaten.
Blend a smoothie of tropical fruit.

practices.name: The ital pot
practices.instructions: Cook one meal today from whole plants only. Start a pot with coconut milk, thyme, spring onion, garlic and allspice, add pumpkin, yam or potato, carrots, greens and beans or peas, and let it simmer until thick. Use herbs for flavour instead of salt. Eat it with thanks, and share a bowl. The rule of this Onda is to eat ital.
practices.why: Ital means pure and natural, and refers to food of the earth, cooked without salt or additives. The ital pot is the heart of Rastafari cooking.
variations: Add dumplings.
Cook outside on a small stove.
Make enough for a neighbour.

practices.name: Hands in the earth
practices.instructions: Spend twenty minutes with living ground. Tend a garden, a pot of herbs or a patch of street soil: weed it, water it, plant something you can eat. If you have none, walk to the nearest trees or water and stay there without a screen. Stay close to the earth, and give a moment of thanks as you leave.
practices.why: Gardening and working the land are central to Rastafari life, which looks to Africa and the earth as a home. Dirt under the fingernails is a good sign.
variations: Plant thyme or callaloo.
Clean the weeds from a neighbour’s path.
Compost today’s scraps.

practices.name: A Babylon-free hour
practices.instructions: For one hour, step away from Babylon in your mind: no news, no ads, no shopping sites, no social feeds. Turn off notifications. Read, make something, talk, walk. Babylon is the Rastafari name for the system that sells you worry and wants. Notice what rises when the noise falls away. The rule of this Onda is not to serve Babylon in your mind.
practices.why: Babylon, in Rastafari speech, is the oppressive system of greed and false values. An hour away from its feeds is a modern way of leaving it for a while.
variations: Do it with a friend.
Read a book outside.
Spend it cooking.

practices.name: Dominoes in the yard
practices.instructions: Play dominoes with friends or family, and slam the tiles down with a flourish, as Jamaicans do. Play to a set score, tease each other and laugh. Make it loud and good-natured. Dominoes is the national game and a fixture of every yard and rum shop. Keep the stakes small, a cup of tea or a bun.
practices.why: Dominoes in Jamaica is a social event full of banter and noise. Playing is a lively way to spend an afternoon with company.
variations: Play ludi instead.
Play with a double-nine set.
Teach a child to play.

practices.name: Make a pot of sorrel
practices.instructions: Steep dried hibiscus sepals, sorrel, in boiling water with ginger and a few cloves or allspice berries. Let it stand for a few hours, strain, sweeten and chill. Serve it cold over ice. The deep red drink is made for Christmas in Jamaica, and is delicious anytime. Pour a glass for someone.
practices.why: Sorrel is a favourite Jamaican drink, made from the hibiscus flower, and a classic of ital living. It is easy to make and beautiful to look at.
variations: Add a slice of orange.
Make a big jug for guests.
Drink it warm on a cold day.

practices.name: Tap out the one drop
practices.instructions: Tap a reggae rhythm on a table: the one drop, where the strong beat falls on three, not one. Count one-two-THREE-four, hitting the table on three with your palm and tapping lightly on the others. Play a reggae record and join in. Add a cymbal or a spoon on the off-beats. It teaches how the music leaves space.
practices.why: The one drop is the heartbeat of roots reggae, made famous by drummer Carlton Barrett. Learning to feel the space is a joy.
variations: Play along to Exodus.
Teach it to a friend.
Tap it on your knee while walking.

practices.name: Heartbeat and reasoning
practices.instructions: Put on Nyabinghi drumming, or tap the heartbeat yourself on a table: two soft beats and a rest, about once a second. Sit with it for five minutes and let your breathing slow. Then reason. With one or more people, take a question, a worry or an idea and talk it through in turns, each speaking without interruption, until you overstand it. Keep it peaceful.
practices.why: Reasoning is a Rastafari sitting for discussion and mutual understanding, often with drumming and chanting. It is a gentle way to think together.
variations: Reason on one proverb.
Reason by candlelight.
Reason with a friend by phone.

practices.name: A Psalm at night
practices.instructions: Before bed, read a psalm aloud or listen to one read. Psalm 23, 91 or 121 are favourites. Read it slowly, and let the words of protection and comfort calm you. Rastafari tradition reads the Psalms every day. Finish by naming one thing you are thankful for and one hope for tomorrow.
practices.why: The Psalms are central to Rastafari reading, as songs of trust and praise. A psalm at bedtime is a comforting way to end the day.
variations: Read the psalm by candlelight.
Read it with a child.
Learn a verse by heart.

practices.name: Sing a roots song
practices.instructions: Sing a roots reggae song with a friend or with a record: Redemption Song, One Love, Satta Massagana or Get Up, Stand Up. Learn the words, harmonise and hold the long notes. Sing out in the evening air. Roots music was the voice of a movement and it sounds best sung together.
practices.why: Roots reggae carries Rastafari message to the world. Singing it is a pleasure, and the words repay attention.
variations: Learn all the verses of one song.
Sing it unplugged with a guitar.
Sing in a different voice.

practices.name: An Anansi story
practices.instructions: Tell or read an Anansi story, the trickster spider tales brought to Jamaica from West Africa. Choose one, such as how Anansi got all the stories from the sky god, and tell it with voices and gestures. Ask the listener to guess what happens next. Anansi tales are told at wakes, in yards and to children everywhere.
practices.why: Anansi stories came with enslaved Africans to the Caribbean and have been told for centuries. They show wit and survival.
variations: Tell it to a child.
Write a new Anansi story.
Tell the story of a clever friend.

practices.name: Give thanks at night
practices.instructions: Before you sleep, write down five things you received today, big or small, and give thanks for each. Say Give thanks and praise. Begin with the plainest: water, food, shelter. In Rastafari livity, thanks are the first and last words of the day. End by wishing every one of the people you met well.
practices.why: Gratitude is the foundation of the Rastafari day. A written list helps it grow.
variations: Say them aloud under the sky.
Include one hard thing you learned.
Thank someone for each item.

practices.name: A dub night
practices.instructions: Dim the lights, put on a dub record by King Tubby, Lee Perry or Augustus Pablo, and listen with headphones or a good speaker. Feel the bass in your chest. Dub is reggae stripped back, with echo and spaces, and made by studio engineers at their mixing desk. Lie back and let the sound move in the room.
practices.why: Dub was invented in Kingston studios in the 1960s and 70s and is the ancestor of much electronic music. Listening deeply is a joy.
variations: Listen with your eyes closed.
Listen with a friend.
Try to hear every echo.

practices.name: An ital feast
practices.instructions: Cook an ital feast for friends: a pot of stew with pumpkin and beans, rice and peas, steamed callaloo, roasted breadfruit or plantain, with sorrel to drink. Serve it outdoors if you can, with music on and everyone helping. Say a word of thanks before eating. Share the cooking, the eating and the washing up.
practices.why: Sharing ital food is a joyful part of Rastafari fellowship. A big pot made together is a feast and a lesson.
variations: Ask each guest to bring a dish.
Cook over a small fire if allowed.
Eat from big shared bowls.

practices.name: A groundation evening
practices.instructions: Hold a gathering in the style of a groundation: friends in a circle under the sky, a drum or simple rhythm, songs, a psalm, a story and reasoning. Keep it peaceful and open to everyone. Begin with thanks and end with blessing. No one need dress up, and no one need join in more than they want to.
practices.why: Groundations are the great gatherings of Rastafari, with Nyabinghi drumming and chanting through the night. A small, respectful version captures the spirit of fellowship.
variations: Hold it outdoors by a small fire.
Share one song or poem each.
Close with a round of blessings.

immersePlan.name: Read a speech of Marcus Garvey
immersePlan.text: Read a short speech or essay by Marcus Garvey, the Jamaican thinker who urged Black pride and self-reliance. Pick one sentence.

immersePlan.name: Read Rastafari: Roots and Ideology
immersePlan.text: Read a chapter of Barry Chevannes’s scholarly account of how Rastafari grew from the Jamaican hills. Note one new fact.

immersePlan.name: Read Brother Man
immersePlan.text: Read a chapter of Roger Mais’s 1954 novel of a gentle Rasta healer in Kingston’s slums. Notice the Jamaican speech.

immersePlan.name: Watch The Harder They Come
immersePlan.text: Watch Perry Henzell’s 1972 film with Jimmy Cliff as a young singer in Kingston. Listen for the soundtrack.

immersePlan.name: Watch Rockers
immersePlan.text: Watch Ted Bafaloukos’s 1978 film with Kingston’s musicians playing themselves, centred on a drummer with a motorbike. It is full of music and joy.

immersePlan.name: Watch Marley
immersePlan.text: Watch Kevin Macdonald’s documentary on Bob Marley, with family and band members. Watch for the early years in Trench Town.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Exodus
immersePlan.text: Play Bob Marley and the Wailers’ 1977 album from start to finish. Sing along to Jamming and One Love.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Satta Massagana
immersePlan.text: Play The Abyssinians’ song of harmony, sung in Amharic. It is among the finest roots records. Hum the bass line.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Grounation
immersePlan.text: Play Count Ossie and the Mystic Revelation of Rastafari’s 1973 album of Nyabinghi drumming and chanting with jazz horns. Let it fill the room.

immersePlan.name: Look at Ras Daniel Heartman’s portraits
immersePlan.text: Look at the fine pencil portraits by Ras Daniel Heartman, with their dignity and detail. Pick one and describe the person.

immersePlan.name: Look at Everald Brown
immersePlan.text: Look at the paintings of Everald Brown, a Jamaican painter and musician whose work is full of lions, hills and visions. Describe the colours.

immersePlan.name: Look at Neville Garrick’s sleeves
immersePlan.text: Look at the cover designs by Neville Garrick for the Wailers’ albums, with their red, gold and green. Choose your favourite.

immersePlan.name: Cook an ital stew
immersePlan.text: Cook a pot of pumpkin, yam, beans and greens in coconut milk with thyme and allspice. Eat with thanks.

immersePlan.name: Make rice and peas
immersePlan.text: Cook rice with kidney beans in coconut milk, thyme, spring onion and a whole scotch bonnet pepper. Do not burst the pepper.

immersePlan.name: Steam callaloo
immersePlan.text: Steam amaranth leaves with onion, tomato and thyme. If you cannot find callaloo, use spinach. Eat it hot with a slice of yam.

immersePlan.name: Drink coconut water
immersePlan.text: Drink from a young green coconut, or from a carton if you must. It is the best cooling drink in the world. Scoop out the jelly with a spoon.

immersePlan.name: Brew a bush tea
immersePlan.text: Steep fresh lemongrass or mint in hot water with a slice of ginger. Sweeten with honey if you like and drink it slowly.

immersePlan.name: Make a jug of sorrel
immersePlan.text: Steep dried hibiscus sepals with ginger, then strain and sweeten. Serve cold over ice.

immersePlan.name: Learn about red, gold and green
immersePlan.text: Read about the red, gold and green, taken from the Ethiopian flag and used by Rastafari and across Africa. As a guest, notice them without wearing them.

immersePlan.name: Greet with a blessing today
immersePlan.text: Greet three people today with a blessing in place of hello: respect, give thanks or blessed love.

immersePlan.name: Learn about locks
immersePlan.text: Read about the Nazirite vow behind the locks in Rastafari, and how they became a symbol of identity. Think about what you wear to say who you are.

immersePlan.name: Play dominoes slam style
immersePlan.text: Play dominoes with friends and slam the tiles on the table with a flourish. Talk loudly, laugh and keep score.

immersePlan.name: Kick a ball about
immersePlan.text: Jamaica loves football. Kick a ball with friends in a yard or park for half an hour, and clap a good move.

immersePlan.name: Play ludi
immersePlan.text: Play ludi, the Jamaican cousin of Ludo, with dice and tokens on a cross-shaped board. Play a quick game with children or friends.

immersePlan.name: Mark Groundation Day
immersePlan.text: Groundation Day, 21 April, marks the 1966 visit to Jamaica of Haile Selassie. Listen to a Nyabinghi drum track and read a short account.

immersePlan.name: Look at the Bob Marley Museum
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of 56 Hope Road, the Kingston house where Marley lived and recorded, now a museum. Pick a room and imagine the music.

immersePlan.name: Mark Ethiopian Christmas
immersePlan.text: Ethiopian Christmas, Genna, is on 7 January. Read about the games and white-clad church services, and share a meal in its spirit.

immersePlan.name: Practise livity
immersePlan.text: Livity is a way of life in harmony with nature. Choose one habit today that brings you closer to the earth.

immersePlan.name: Practise overstand
immersePlan.text: Overstand means to grasp a thing deeply. Take one idea you think you understand and look at it from above and below.

immersePlan.name: Say irie
immersePlan.text: Irie means all is well. Say it once today when you really mean it, and look for what is well.

rules.why: Begin the day with praise, spoken aloud, before news or messages.
Whole food from the earth. Nothing dead, nothing processed, as far as you can keep it.
Speak life. Do not curse yourself or anyone else, even in jest.

rules.text: Do not serve Babylon in your mind
rules.why: Notice where greed, status and fear are doing your thinking, and refuse them.
Touch soil, water or trees every day.

rules.text: Meet every person as I and I
rules.why: The same life is in them as in you. Greet them as an equal.

read.title: The Kebra Nagast
read.creator: trans. E. A. Wallis Budge
read.why: The Glory of Kings: the Ethiopian national epic, which tells how Solomon and the Queen of Sheba founded the royal line that ended with Haile Selassie.

read.title: Philosophy and Opinions of Marcus Garvey
read.creator: ed. Amy Jacques Garvey
read.why: Speeches and articles by the man Rastafari honour as a prophet, collected by his wife while he was in prison.

read.title: Rastafari: Roots and Ideology
read.creator: Barry Chevannes
read.why: A Jamaican anthropologist’s account, built on long conversations with the elders who were there at the start.

read.title: Brother Man
read.creator: Roger Mais
read.why: A novel of the Kingston slums with a gentle Rastafari healer at its centre. The first sympathetic portrait in fiction.

read.title: The Children of Sisyphus
read.creator: Orlando Patterson
read.why: A bleak, vivid novel set on the Kingston rubbish tip called the Dungle, where the poor wait for the ships to Africa.

read.title: Catch a Fire: The Life of Bob Marley
read.creator: Timothy White
read.why: The standard biography, with a long opening on Ethiopia, Garvey and the Jamaica that made the music.

watch.title: Rockers
watch.creator: Ted Bafaloukos
watch.why: A drummer’s motorbike is stolen and he gets even. The cast are the real musicians of roots reggae, speaking their own language.

watch.title: The Harder They Come
watch.creator: Perry Henzell
watch.why: A country boy comes to Kingston to be a singer and becomes an outlaw. The film that carried reggae abroad.

watch.title: Countryman
watch.creator: Dickie Jobson
watch.why: A fisherman who lives by nature’s law hides two crash survivors. A fable of livity, played by a real Rastafari fisherman.

watch.title: Marley
watch.creator: Kevin Macdonald
watch.why: A full documentary life, made with the family, with rare footage and the people who knew him.

listen.title: Grounation
listen.creator: Count Ossie and the Mystic Revelation of Rastafari
listen.why: Three records of Nyabinghi drums, horns, chant and spoken history. The nearest a recording comes to a gathering in the hills.

listen.title: Marcus Garvey
listen.creator: Burning Spear
listen.why: Winston Rodney’s deep, dry voice calls up the prophet and the slave ships. A cornerstone of roots reggae.

listen.title: Satta Massagana
listen.creator: The Abyssinians
listen.why: The title song, partly in Amharic, became an anthem sung almost as a hymn.

listen.title: Exodus
listen.creator: Bob Marley and the Wailers
listen.why: Recorded in London after an attempt on his life. The first side is the movement of Jah people set to music.

listen.title: Two Sevens Clash
listen.creator: Culture
listen.why: Joseph Hill sings a Garvey prophecy about the seventh of July 1977. Kingston shut its shops on the day.

art.title: Pencil portraits of Rastafari
art.creator: Ras Daniel Heartman
art.why: Finely drawn heads of locksmen and children, sold as prints across Jamaica. The first images in which the movement saw its own dignity.

art.title: Ethiopian Apple and other paintings
art.creator: Everald Brown
art.why: A self-taught visionary and Ethiopian Orthodox elder who painted the hills full of hidden figures and built his own instruments.

art.title: The imperial standard of Ethiopia
art.creator: Ethiopian court workshops
art.why: Green, gold and red with the crowned Lion of Judah carrying a cross-topped staff. The source of the colours seen everywhere in the movement.

art.title: Album sleeves for Bob Marley and the Wailers
art.creator: Neville Garrick
art.why: Rastaman Vibration, Exodus and Survival. Garrick brought Ethiopian lettering and the flags of Africa to record shops worldwide.

eat.title: Ital stew
eat.creator: Pumpkin, yam, beans and greens in coconut milk with thyme and allspice
eat.why: The one-pot meal of the movement, seasoned with herbs and hot pepper and little or no salt.

eat.title: Rice and peas
eat.creator: Rice with kidney beans or gungo peas, coconut milk and thyme
eat.why: The Sunday dish of all Jamaica, and ital as it stands.

eat.title: Callaloo
eat.creator: Steamed amaranth leaves with onion, tomato and pepper
eat.why: A dark green leaf grown in every yard. Eaten at breakfast with boiled green banana.

eat.title: Roast breadfruit
eat.creator: A whole breadfruit turned over coals until black, then peeled
eat.why: Smoky and filling, and eaten by hand. Breadfruit trees feed whole districts in season.

drink.title: Coconut water
drink.creator: Drunk from a green jelly coconut
drink.why: Sold at the roadside and opened with a machete. Clean water straight from the tree.

drink.title: Bush tea
drink.creator: Fever grass, mint, or bitter cerasee, steeped in hot water
drink.why: Jamaican herb teas taken in the morning. Fever grass is lemongrass.

drink.title: Sorrel
drink.creator: Hibiscus sepals steeped with ginger and pimento
drink.why: A deep red drink made at Christmas. Leave out the rum.

drink.title: Fresh juice
drink.creator: Soursop, june plum, or carrot blended with water and lime
drink.why: Ital shops sell juices made to order with nothing added.

customs.title: The colours
customs.creator: Red, gold and green, and often black
customs.why: From the Ethiopian flag and from Garvey’s movement. Commonly read as blood, wealth and the land, with black for the people.

customs.title: Locks and the covered head
customs.creator: The Nazirite vow
customs.why: Many Rastafari let their hair grow uncut and matted and cover it with a knitted tam or a wrap. The locks are a covenant, and visitors should not treat them as a style to try on.

customs.title: Greeting with blessing
customs.creator: Blessed love; Give thanks; One love
customs.why: Words of greeting and parting are blessings. Among the brethren a fist is touched to a fist and then to the heart.

customs.title: The herb
customs.creator: A sacrament of some houses
customs.why: Cannabis is smoked by many Rastafari as an aid to reasoning and prayer, with a blessing first. It is a rite of the community and is not part of this Onda.

games.title: Dominoes
games.creator: Table game · Jamaica
games.why: Played in fours, in partners, and slammed down hard. The game of every yard and rum-free ital shop on the island.

games.title: Football
games.creator: Team sport
games.why: Bob Marley played every day he could, on tour and at Hope Road. Roots musicians and footballers shared the same yards.

games.title: Ludi
games.creator: Board game · Jamaica
games.why: The Jamaican form of ludo, played on large hand-painted wooden boards with two dice.

festivals.title: Groundation Day
festivals.creator: 21 April
festivals.why: The day in 1966 when Haile Selassie landed at Kingston. Marked with Nyabinghi drumming and chant.

festivals.title: The Birthday of His Imperial Majesty
festivals.creator: 23 July
festivals.why: Born in 1892 at Ejersa Goro in Ethiopia. One of the largest gatherings of the year.

festivals.title: Coronation Day
festivals.creator: 2 November
festivals.why: The crowning in Addis Ababa in 1930, the event from which the movement dates itself.

festivals.title: Ethiopian Christmas
festivals.creator: 7 January
festivals.why: Lidät in Ethiopia. Kept with a binghi and an ital feast.

places.title: Bob Marley Museum
places.creator: 56 Hope Road, Kingston, Jamaica
places.why: His home and studio from 1975, kept much as he left it. The tour is led by people who know the music well.

places.title: Rastafari Indigenous Village
places.creator: Montego River Gardens, near Montego Bay, Jamaica
places.why: A living community that receives visitors for drumming, ital food and conversation. Book ahead.

places.title: Pinnacle
places.creator: Sligoville, St Catherine, Jamaica
places.why: The hilltop where Leonard Howell built the first Rastafari community in 1940. Ruins and a wide view remain, and part of the land is protected.

places.title: Shashamane
places.creator: Oromia, Ethiopia
places.why: Land the Emperor granted in 1948 to people of African descent who wished to return. A small Rastafari settlement lives there still.

places.title: Holy Trinity Cathedral
places.creator: Addis Ababa, Ethiopia
places.why: Haile Selassie and Empress Menen are buried here in granite tombs. An Ethiopian Orthodox church: dress modestly and take off your shoes.

ethics.title: Dignity
ethics.text: The movement began by telling the poorest black Jamaicans that they were sons and daughters of kings. Every person is to be met as royal.
ethics.practice: Carry yourself today as someone whose worth is not in question, and grant the same to each person you meet.

ethics.title: Natural living
ethics.text: The body is a temple and the earth is a gift. What is closest to how it grew is best.
ethics.practice: Replace one manufactured thing in your day with its natural form.

ethics.title: Truth in speech
ethics.text: Words make and unmake. Lies, flattery and curses do harm in the world.
ethics.practice: Say nothing today that you do not mean.

ethics.title: Justice
ethics.text: Equal rights and justice is a constant demand. Peace without them is only quiet.
ethics.practice: Find one unfairness within your reach and act on it.

ethics.title: Sharing
ethics.text: At Pinnacle and in the camps food was held in common. What Jah gives is for all.
ethics.practice: Share a meal today with someone who did not expect it.

ethics.title: Love
ethics.text: One love means one human family under one Creator. It is asked of the oppressed towards one another first, and then towards everyone.
ethics.practice: Settle one quarrel, or take the first step.

philosophy.title: I and I
philosophy.text: Jah lives within each person. There is no you set against me, only I and I. The grammar itself refuses to let anyone be an object.
philosophy.practice: For one conversation today, think of the other person as I.

philosophy.title: Babylon and Zion
philosophy.text: History is read as captivity and return. Babylon is every system that lives off others, and Zion is the home and the rightness from which people were taken.
philosophy.practice: Name one thing in your life that belongs to Babylon, and one that belongs to Zion.

philosophy.title: Mental slavery
philosophy.text: Chains came off the body in 1838. The harder work is to free a mind taught to despise itself.
philosophy.practice: Trace one belief about yourself back to who taught it to you.

philosophy.title: Word, sound and power
philosophy.text: Language is not neutral. To rename a thing is to see it differently, and to speak is to act.
philosophy.practice: Change one word you use for yourself.

philosophy.title: Livity
philosophy.text: Faith is a way of living more than a set of beliefs. It shows in the pot, the garden, the greeting and the day’s work.
philosophy.practice: Ask of one ordinary act today: does this give life?

philosophy.title: The living God
philosophy.text: Rastafari look for God in a living person and in this world. Many hold Haile Selassie to be the returned Christ. Others see him as a king chosen by God.
philosophy.practice: Where do you look for the sacred: far off, or in front of you?

philosophy.title: Know your history
philosophy.text: A people cut off from their past can be told anything. Learning African history is a religious duty.
philosophy.practice: Learn the story of one ancestor, or one event your schooling left out.

philosophy.title: Repatriation
philosophy.text: To go home. For some it means ships to Africa. For others it means building Zion where they stand and carrying Africa within.
philosophy.practice: Ask where home is for you, and what it would take to live there.

journal: Where did Babylon get into your head today?
What did you give thanks for this morning?
What did you eat today that was alive?
Which of your words did harm?
Whom did you treat as separate from you?
What do you believe about yourself that someone else put there?
Where is Zion for you?
What part of your history were you never taught?
When did you feel like royalty today?
Whom did you look down on?
What did the earth give you today?
What are you still a slave to?
Which word would you rebuild?
Where did you keep quiet for the sake of peace without justice?
What would you do if you were not afraid of the system?
Whom do you call brother or sister, and mean it?
What did the drum do to your breathing?
What did you learn by reasoning that you could not learn alone?
Where did you see Jah in a person today?
What are you growing?
What did you buy that you did not need?
Who are your ancestors, and what did they survive?
What vow would you keep for life?
What does your body tell you about how you are living?
Whose labour made your day possible?
What would freedom of mind look like tomorrow?
What song carried you today?
What does one love ask of you this week?
Where do you feel in exile?
What are you carrying home?

What did eating ital teach you about your habits?
Which words have you stopped using?
Where do you now see Babylon that you did not before?
What did reasoning with others open up?
What part of this livity will you keep?

intro: Rastafari began in Jamaica in the early 1930s. The island was a British colony. Slavery had ended less than a century before, and most of the descendants of the enslaved were landless, poor and taught at school and in church that everything good was white. Against this stood Marcus Garvey, a Jamaican printer who had built the largest black movement in history, told his people to be proud of Africa and to look there for their redemption.

In November 1930 a nobleman named Ras Tafari Makonnen was crowned Emperor of Ethiopia as Haile Selassie I, King of Kings and Conquering Lion of the Tribe of Judah. Ethiopia was an ancient Christian kingdom, never colonised, whose rulers claimed descent from Solomon and the Queen of Sheba. Princes came from Europe to bow at the coronation. In Jamaica, several street preachers who knew their Bibles, Leonard Howell first among them, read the news with the Book of Revelation open and concluded that the promised king had come, and that God was black.

The colonial authorities jailed Howell for sedition. On his release he founded a community at Pinnacle, in the hills, where several thousand people farmed and lived in common until the police broke it up in the 1950s. Its people scattered into the Kingston slums and took the movement with them. There a younger generation grew their hair into locks, shaped a way of speaking of their own, and worked out the practice of drumming, chanting and reasoning.

For thirty years Rastafari were despised, beaten and shaved by the police. Two things changed their standing. In April 1966 Haile Selassie visited Jamaica, and a crowd of a hundred thousand met him at the airport. And in the 1970s the musicians of Kingston, Bob Marley above all, carried the message around the world in reggae.

Rastafari has no church, no creed and no head. Its main houses, or mansions, are the Nyabinghi Order, the Bobo Ashanti and the Twelve Tribes of Israel, and many belong to none. What is shared is a reading of the Bible from the side of the captive, reverence for Haile Selassie, love of Africa, a natural way of life called livity, and refusal of Babylon, the system that lives off the poor. There may be around a million Rastafari today, in the Caribbean, Africa, Europe, the Americas and Japan.

This Onda follows a day of livity: thanks at sunrise, careful speech, an ital pot, hands in the earth and reasoning to the heartbeat drum. You are a guest. The movement was made by people of African descent out of their own history of slavery, and its sacraments, its locks and its faith in the Emperor are theirs. What it offers anyone is a clear look at what rules the mind, and a simpler way to live.
guide.origin: Jamaica, among the poor of Kingston and the eastern parishes, looking towards Ethiopia
guide.era: From the crowning of Haile Selassie in 1930 to the present day

figures.name: Marcus Garvey
figures.bio: Jamaican founder of the Universal Negro Improvement Association and the Black Star Line. He was not a Rastafari and criticised the Emperor, yet the movement honours him as its John the Baptist.

figures.name: Haile Selassie I
figures.bio: Emperor of Ethiopia from 1930 to 1974. He resisted the Italian invasion, helped found the Organisation of African Unity, and remained a devout Ethiopian Orthodox Christian who never claimed divinity.

figures.name: Empress Menen Asfaw
figures.bio: Crowned beside her husband in 1930. Rastafari women honour her as the model of the Empress, and her birthday is kept in some houses.

figures.name: Leonard Howell
figures.bio: Often called the first Rasta. He travelled widely, began preaching the divinity of the Emperor in 1933, was jailed for sedition and founded Pinnacle.

figures.name: Joseph Hibbert
figures.bio: One of the first preachers, who had lived in Costa Rica and brought an interest in Ethiopian mystical lore.

figures.name: Mortimo Planno
figures.bio: A Nyabinghi elder and a member of the 1961 mission to Africa. He calmed the crowd at the airport in 1966 and later taught Bob Marley.

figures.name: Prince Emmanuel Charles Edwards
figures.bio: Founder of the Bobo Ashanti, a strict priestly order that lives in community at Bull Bay, wears turbans and robes and keeps the Sabbath.

figures.name: Vernon Carrington, the Prophet Gad
figures.bio: Founder in 1968 of the Twelve Tribes of Israel, the most open of the mansions, which encourages daily Bible reading and counted many musicians as members.

figures.name: Count Ossie
figures.bio: The master drummer whose camp in the Wareika Hills brought Nyabinghi rhythm together with jazz players and shaped Jamaican popular music.

figures.name: Bob Marley
figures.bio: Singer and songwriter from Nine Mile who made the movement known on every continent. He was baptised into the Ethiopian Orthodox Church shortly before his death.

history.detail: In Kingston. Within a few years it has millions of followers across the Americas and Africa, a newspaper and a shipping line.
Ras Tafari is crowned Haile Selassie I in Addis Ababa. Photographs appear in newspapers worldwide and reach Jamaica.
He sells pictures of the Emperor as passports to Ethiopia and tells crowds they owe the British king nothing. He is sentenced to two years for sedition.
Mussolini’s army uses poison gas. The Emperor appeals to the League of Nations in vain, goes into exile in England and returns with Allied help. Black people worldwide rally to Ethiopia.
Howell buys an abandoned estate above Sligoville. For over a decade it is a self-governing community, raided again and again.
The Emperor sets aside land for black people of the West who supported Ethiopia in the war. The first settlers arrive in the 1950s.
Police raze the settlement. Its people move to the shanty towns of west Kingston, where the dreadlocks and the Nyabinghi drumming take form.
At the request of Rastafari elders, three scholars of the University College of the West Indies study the movement and urge the government to stop the persecution and send a mission to Africa.
After a violent incident near Montego Bay the government orders a round-up. Hundreds of Rastafari are beaten, shorn and jailed. The day is remembered as Bad Friday, and the state apologised in 2017.
The crowd on the tarmac is so great that Haile Selassie stays in the aircraft until Mortimo Planno is asked to make a way. Rastafari elders are received at King’s House for the first time.
The Wailers’ Catch a Fire opens a decade in which the music takes the message to Africa, Europe and the Pacific.

history.what: The fall and death of the Emperor
history.detail: A military committee deposes Haile Selassie in a year of famine. He dies in custody in August 1975. Many Rastafari do not accept that he could die.
Possession of small amounts of cannabis is decriminalised, and Rastafari are granted the right to use it as a sacrament.

concepts.detail: God is not a spirit in the sky. For most Rastafari he was revealed in the person of Haile Selassie, and he dwells within every human being.
Named after the empire that carried Israel into captivity. It covers slavery, colonial rule and their heirs in government, commerce, police and church.
Ethiopia stands for all Africa, the land from which the ancestors were taken. Zion is also the condition of living rightly, which can begin anywhere.
The first person replaces the others. It asserts the speaker’s dignity, the presence of Jah within, and the bond between people.
The daily discipline of natural food, clean speech, honest work and praise. More weight is placed on how one lives than on what one professes.
Rules differ between houses, but the direction is always towards plants, freshness and simplicity, and away from meat, salt, alcohol and anything processed.
Words carry force through their sound. Iyaric, the movement’s speech, removes sounds of defeat from English and plants I throughout.
From John 14:2. The Nyabinghi Order, the Bobo Ashanti and the Twelve Tribes of Israel differ in dress, discipline and doctrine. None can speak for all.
The original and still living demand that the descendants of enslaved Africans be returned home, as a right and at the cost of those who took them.

facts.text: The name Haile Selassie means Power of the Trinity. It is a baptismal name he took as his throne name.
Ethiopia is the only African country that defeated a European army in the Scramble for Africa, at Adwa in 1896.
The funde drum plays close to the pace of a resting heart, and Nyabinghi chant is slower than any other Jamaican music.
The one-drop rhythm of reggae, with the weight on the third beat, grew out of studio drummers who had played in Rastafari camps.
Slavery in Jamaica ended fully on 1 August 1838, still kept as Emancipation Day.
Haile Selassie gave a gold medal to each of the Rastafari elders he received in 1966.

sensitivity.note: Rastafari is a living faith born from the experience of slavery and colonial rule in Jamaica. This Onda borrows its daily livity: praise, ital food, careful speech and reasoning. It does not ask you to wear locks or colours, to use its sacrament or to claim its identity.
requiredCaveats: Dreadlocks are a religious covenant for Rastafari. They are not a costume, and the people who wear them have been beaten and jailed for it.
Rastafari was made by people of African descent out of their own history. A guest should listen more than speak.
The mansions differ on doctrine, on the Bible and on who Haile Selassie is. No summary speaks for all of them.
Cannabis is a sacrament in some houses and is illegal in many countries. It is left out of the practices here.
